item.title: Population-averaged predictions from multilevel probit models
item.dc:creator: Marco Steenbergen
item.description:
Population-Averaging

In multilevel analysis, we often interpret the results through population-averaging. Population averaging removes all of the disturbances from the model by averaging them out. In a linear model this is straightforward. Consider, for instance, the random intercept model for level-1 units nested in level-2 units (e.g., individuals in countries): The standard assumption in the random intercept model is that the level-2 disturbances, , have an expectation of 0 and that the same is true of the level-1 disturbances, . Hence, averaging across both units, we obtain .

Averaging Gone Wrong

Population-averaging can also be applied to multilevel models for binary dependent variables. An example is the multilevel probit model with a random intercept. Let the binary variable equal 1 if the latent variable is greater than or equal to 0, and 0 otherwise. For the latent variable, we assume

with , , and . Consequently,

where is the cumulative standard normal distribution function. Figure 1 shows the probability curve for . The curve is concave for and convex for . This becomes important for our discussion later.

When we population-average the predicted probability, I continue to see a common mistake: users compute . In that approach, the fact that and the assumption that the level-2 errors have an expectation of 0, results in a proposed population-averaged predicted probability of . That is false! In this blog, I show why it is false and how population-averaging is done right.

The Bias

The quantity of interest is not but . This something quite different, because is a nonlinear function. The curvature in Figure 1 gives the intuition. To the right of 0, is concave, so averaging over the spread in pulls the expected probability below . To the left of 0, is convex, and the expected probability is pulled above . Only at 0 do the two coincide.

This is only an intuition, however. Jensen’s inequality proper requires the function to be concave (or convex) over the entire support of the random variable. Because is normal, ranges over the whole real line, and so spreads mass over both the concave and the convex part of the curve. The net effect therefore requires an exact calculation, which we turn to now. Plugging in either over- or under-estimates the probability, depending on the sign of the linear predictor.

Let us assess the bias for a very simple model where ; analogous to a random effects ANOVA, we have a constant only. If we plug in a value of zero for , corresponding to its expectation, we obtain

The actual population-averaged estimator is

Since and are assumed to be statistically independent and are both normal, their sum is normal with mean 0 and variance . The double integral is therefore simply , so that

The bias from plugging in is thus

Dividing by pulls the argument toward 0, so the plug-in probability is too extreme: too high when , too low when , and correct only when . For and , for instance, the plug-in is , whereas the population-averaged probability is .

See the Bias

The sliders in Figure 2 set the level-2 variance and the constant . The dashed curve is the plug-in probability , the solid curve is the population-averaged probability , and the shaded area between them is the bias. At the two curves coincide. As grows, the population-averaged curve flattens toward 0.5.

Show code 
viewof tau = Inputs.range([0, 9], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "τ₀₀ (level-2 variance)"})
viewof gam = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "γ₀₀"})
Show code 
Phi = {
  const erf = (x) => {
    const s = Math.sign(x), a = Math.abs(x);
    const t = 1 / (1 + 0.3275911 * a);
    const y = 1 - (((((1.061405429 * t - 1.453152027) * t) + 1.421413741) * t - 0.284496736) * t + 0.254829592) * t * Math.exp(-a * a);
    return s * y;
  };
  return (x) => 0.5 * (1 + erf(x / Math.SQRT2));
}

grid = d3.range(-4, 4.001, 0.05).map(g => ({
  g, plugin: Phi(g), popavg: Phi(g / Math.sqrt(1 + tau))
}))

pPlug = Phi(gam)
pPop = Phi(gam / Math.sqrt(1 + tau))
Show code 
Plot.plot({
  width: 520,
  height: 340,
  style: {background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "γ₀₀", domain: [-4, 4]},
  y: {label: "Pr(y = 1)", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "2 3"}),
    Plot.areaY(grid, {x: "g", y1: "plugin", y2: "popavg", fill: "#c97b2a", fillOpacity: 0.35}),
    Plot.line(grid, {x: "g", y: "plugin", stroke: "#1f2318", strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
    Plot.line(grid, {x: "g", y: "popavg", stroke: "#1f2318", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([gam], {stroke: "#c97b2a"}),
    Plot.dot([{y: pPlug}, {y: pPop}], {x: gam, y: "y", fill: "#c97b2a", r: 4})
  ]
})
Show code 
html`<p>At γ₀₀ = ${gam.toFixed(1)} and τ₀₀ = ${tau.toFixed(2)}: plug-in = ${pPlug.toFixed(3)},
population-averaged = ${pPop.toFixed(3)}, bias =
${((pPlug - pPop) * 100).toFixed(1)} percentage points.</p>`

A Simulation

A constant-only model is a stylized case, so let us check the result in a more realistic setting with two predictors, (the predictor of interest) and a binary . The data-generating process is

with , , , and . There are 300 level-2 units with 40 level-1 units each. We hold constant at 0 and plot the probability as a function of . The dashed curve plugs in . The solid curve is the population-averaged probability, computed with the closed form from the previous section, using the estimated coefficients and variance. The points are the observed shares of ones at each value of among units with , which require no model at all.

Setup: parameters, data generation, plotting 
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)

g00 <- -0.5; g10 <- 1; g20 <- 0.8; tau00 <- 1.5
J <- 300; n <- 40; N <- J * n

simulate_data <- function(link) {
  d <- tibble(
    j  = rep(1:J, each = n),
    x1 = sample(-3:3, N, replace = TRUE),
    x2 = rbinom(N, 1, 0.5)
  )
  delta <- rnorm(J, 0, sqrt(tau00))
  e <- if (link == "probit") rnorm(N) else rlogis(N)
  d$y <- as.integer(g00 + g10 * d$x1 + g20 * d$x2 + delta[d$j] + e >= 0)
  d
}

# Observed share of ones by x1 among units with x2 = 0
observed <- function(d) {
  d |>
    filter(x2 == 0) |>
    group_by(x1) |>
    summarise(p = mean(y), se = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n()), .groups = "drop")
}

plot_sim <- function(curves, emp) {
  long <- curves |>
    pivot_longer(-x1, names_to = "type", values_to = "p") |>
    mutate(type = factor(type, levels = c("plug_in", "pop_avg", "approx"),
                         labels = c("Plug-in", "Population-averaged",
                                    "Approximation")))
  ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = long, aes(x1, p, linetype = type),
              colour = "#1f2318", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_pointrange(data = emp,
                    aes(x1, p, ymin = p - 1.96 * se, ymax = p + 1.96 * se),
                    colour = "#c97b2a") +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Plug-in" = "dashed",
                                     "Population-averaged" = "solid",
                                     "Approximation" = "dotted")) +
    labs(x = expression(x[1]), y = "Pr(y = 1)", linetype = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#faf7f2", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#faf7f2", colour = NA)
    )
}
Show code 
set.seed(2026)
d <- simulate_data("probit")

fit <- glmer(y ~ x1 + x2 + (1 | j), data = d,
             family = binomial(link = "probit"), nAGQ = 10)
b <- fixef(fit)
tau_hat <- as.numeric(VarCorr(fit)$j)

curves <- tibble(x1 = seq(-3, 3, 0.05)) |>
  mutate(eta     = b["(Intercept)"] + b["x1"] * x1,   # x2 held at 0
         plug_in = pnorm(eta),
         pop_avg = pnorm(eta / sqrt(1 + tau_hat))) |>
  select(-eta)

plot_sim(curves, observed(d))

The points in Figure 3 follow the solid curve and depart from the dashed one. The plug-in curve is too steep: it is too low for small values of and too high for large values, and the two curves cross where the probability is close to 0.5. This is the same pattern as in the constant-only case, now with a covariate, and it is not an artifact of estimation: the solid curve is computed from the fitted model and the points are not.

A Random Slope

The next step is to let the effect of vary across level-2 units:

with bivariate normal with variances and and covariance . The closed form survives. Conditional on , the composite error is still normal with mean 0, and its variance is . Hence

The attenuation now depends on . The variance in the denominator is a quadratic in with its minimum at , so it grows as moves away from that point, and the population-averaged curve flattens more in the tails than in the random-intercept case. The plug-in curve ignores all of this.

The data below are generated with and . Here I estimate the model in a Bayesian setup with brms. The population-averaged probability is computed separately for each posterior draw and then summarized, so the band reflects uncertainty in the coefficients and in the variance components. Plugging posterior means into the formula would be a Bayesian version of the same mistake as before, because the curve is nonlinear in the parameters.

Show code 
library(brms)

tau11 <- 0.5; tau01 <- 0.3
Sigma <- matrix(c(tau00, tau01, tau01, tau11), 2)

set.seed(2028)
u <- MASS::mvrnorm(J, c(0, 0), Sigma)
d <- tibble(j  = rep(1:J, each = n),
            x1 = sample(-3:3, N, replace = TRUE),
            x2 = rbinom(N, 1, 0.5)) |>
  mutate(y = as.integer(g00 + g10 * x1 + g20 * x2 +
                          u[j, 1] + u[j, 2] * x1 + rnorm(N) >= 0))

fit_rs <- brm(y ~ x1 + x2 + (1 + x1 | j), data = d,
              family = bernoulli(link = "probit"),
              prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2), class = b),
                        prior(normal(0, 2), class = Intercept),
                        prior(exponential(1), class = sd),
                        prior(lkj(2), class = cor)),
              chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2500, seed = 2028, refresh = 0)

dr  <- as_draws_df(fit_rs)
t00 <- dr$sd_j__Intercept^2
t11 <- dr$sd_j__x1^2
t01 <- dr$cor_j__Intercept__x1 * dr$sd_j__Intercept * dr$sd_j__x1

curves <- map_dfr(seq(-3, 3, 0.1), \(x) {
  eta <- dr$b_Intercept + dr$b_x1 * x            # x2 held at 0
  pa  <- pnorm(eta / sqrt(1 + t00 + 2 * t01 * x + t11 * x^2))
  tibble(x1 = x, plug_in = median(pnorm(eta)), pop_avg = median(pa),
         lo = quantile(pa, 0.025), hi = quantile(pa, 0.975))
})

emp <- d |>
  filter(x2 == 0) |>
  group_by(x1) |>
  summarise(p = mean(y), se = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n()), .groups = "drop")

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = curves, aes(x1, ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
              fill = "#1f2318", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(x1, plug_in, linetype = "Plug-in"),
            colour = "#1f2318", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(x1, pop_avg, linetype = "Population-averaged"),
            colour = "#1f2318", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_pointrange(data = emp,
                  aes(x1, p, ymin = p - 1.96 * se, ymax = p + 1.96 * se),
                  colour = "#c97b2a") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Plug-in" = "dashed",
                                   "Population-averaged" = "solid")) +
  labs(x = expression(x[1]), y = "Pr(y = 1)", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#faf7f2", colour = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#faf7f2", colour = NA)
  )

The bias (see Figure 4) is now much larger than in the random-intercept model, and it is not confined to the extremes: at the plug-in probability is about 0.92, whereas the population-averaged probability is about 0.72. The observed shares of ones follow the population-averaged curve throughout.

Extensions

The closed form above rests on two features of the probit model: the level-1 error is normal, and so is the random intercept, so their sum is normal as well. Change either and the integral loses its closed form. The most common case is the multilevel logit model. In the random intercept logit model, for instance, the population-averaged probability is , which has no analytical solution. The bias is the same in kind (the plug-in probability is too extreme), but now it has to be computed numerically. A rough approximation is available because the logistic curve is close to a rescaled probit curve, which gives , but this is an approximation, not an identity.

We repeat the analysis from Figure 3, now using the logit link. The solid curve from Figure 3 can no longer be written in closed form, so we integrate over the random intercept numerically, using the estimated coefficients and variance. The dotted curve is the rescaled-probit approximation from above.

Show code 
set.seed(2027)
d <- simulate_data("logit")

fit <- glmer(y ~ x1 + x2 + (1 | j), data = d,
             family = binomial(link = "logit"), nAGQ = 10)
b <- fixef(fit)
tau_hat <- as.numeric(VarCorr(fit)$j)

# No closed form: integrate the inverse logit over the random intercept
pop_avg_logit <- function(eta, tau) {
  sapply(eta, function(e)
    integrate(function(delta) plogis(e + delta) * dnorm(delta, 0, sqrt(tau)),
              -Inf, Inf)$value)
}

curves <- tibble(x1 = seq(-3, 3, 0.05)) |>
  mutate(eta     = b["(Intercept)"] + b["x1"] * x1,   # x2 held at 0
         plug_in = plogis(eta),
         pop_avg = pop_avg_logit(eta, tau_hat),
         approx  = plogis(eta / sqrt(1 + 0.346 * tau_hat))) |>
  select(-eta)

plot_sim(curves, observed(d))

The picture in Figure 5 is qualitatively the same as in the probit case: the plug-in curve is too extreme relative to the population-averaged curve. The dotted approximation is hard to tell apart from the solid curve, but note that only the numerical integral is exact.

The brmsmargins package does the numerical integration for models fit with brms. It computes marginal predictions, average marginal effects, and population-averaged (“marginal”) coefficients, integrating the random effects out of each posterior draw by simulation. It therefore works for any link function, for random slopes, and for models with several random effects. The sketch below is kept simple; see the package vignette on mixed effects models for the full set of arguments.

Show code 
library(brms)
library(brmsmargins)

fit <- brm(y ~ x1 + x2 + (1 + x1 | j), data = d,
           family = bernoulli(link = "logit"))

# Average predicted probability over x1, integrating out the random effects
brmsmargins(fit,
            at = data.frame(x1 = seq(-3, 3, 0.5), x2 = 0),
            effects = "integrateoutRE", k = 100, seed = 1234)

For the probit model with normal random effects, I would still use the closed form: it is exact, instantaneous, and shows where the bias comes from. Use brmsmargins when the closed form is not available, or when you want average marginal effects rather than predicted probabilities.
